title: Floating Cinema Brings Bollywood Classics to Srinagar's Dal Lake
excerpt: Srinagar's Dal Lake became an open-air cinema as the inaugural Jammu & Kashmir film festival screened Bollywood classics to audiences on shikaras and the lakefront.
body:
• The inaugural International Film Festival of Jammu & Kashmir (September 7–10, 2026) set up a floating cinema on Srinagar's Dal Lake, with audiences watching from the lakefront and in shikaras.
  • The program opened on September 7 with the 1961 Shammi Kapoor classic Junglee, followed by Arzoo (1965) and Kashmir Ki Kali (1964), with Yash Chopra's Kabhi Kabhie (1976) scheduled for the closing day.
  • The festival selected 135 films from more than 40 countries out of roughly 1,100 submissions from 92 countries, drawing over 360 delegates from outside J&K.
  • The floating screen revives a 2021 experiment — Dal Lake's first open-air floating theatre — and is being watched as a possible permanent addition to Kashmir's cultural calendar.

Bollywood Classics Under Open Sky at Dal Lake

Srinagar's Dal Lake became an open-air cinema hall this week as the first International Film Festival of Jammu & Kashmir (IFFJK) brought its floating cinema to the water. A giant screen was installed over the lake near the Sher-e-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC), the festival's main venue, while viewers gathered along the lakefront and in shikaras — the dark water, mountain silhouettes and Srinagar's evening lights forming a backdrop no auditorium could replicate.

The initiative opened on September 7 with a screening of Junglee, the 1961 Shammi Kapoor classic. The choice was deliberate: the film belongs to the era when Kashmir was becoming one of Hindi cinema's most filmed destinations, so the audience sat in the very landscape that helped establish the Valley's relationship with Bollywood. Subsequent screenings included Arzoo (1965) and Kashmir Ki Kali (1964), with Yash Chopra's Kabhi Kabhie (1976) scheduled for the festival's concluding day, September 10.

Officials said the floating screen was designed to give the inaugural festival a signature experience: viewers seated on shikaras can watch films against the lake itself, turning Kashmir's landscape from a backdrop into part of the show.

Context & Background

The four-day IFFJK, themed "Rang-e-Cinema," is organized by the J&K Department of Information and Public Relations and runs across Srinagar, Jammu, Gulmarg and the city's Inox multiplex. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah inaugurated the festival at SKICC on September 7. The lineup spans international and regional cinema alongside masterclasses and workshops aimed at students, aspiring filmmakers and local cinema enthusiasts, with 135 films chosen from about 1,100 submissions from 92 countries.

The floating cinema has a predecessor. In October 2021, the J&K administration launched Dal Lake's first open-air floating theatre during its Iconic Week celebrations, inaugurated by then Chief Secretary Arun Kumar Mehta — and the opening screening then was also Kashmir Ki Kali. Tourism officials at the time framed it as an evening-activity product for visitors.

"We have a great demand for evening activities. The concept of open-air is pretty unique, not found anywhere in this world. It will greatly advantage the tourism in Kashmir."

— Sarmad Hafeez, Secretary, Tourism and Culture, J&K, to ANI (2021)

Impact & Analysis

Kashmir's association with Hindi cinema runs deep — Dal Lake, Gulmarg and Pahalgam became visual shorthand for romance in generations of Indian films — but that relationship thinned as production patterns changed and alternative destinations emerged. IFFJK is an explicit attempt to reverse that trend: officials want the festival to restore filmmakers' confidence and draw productions back to the Valley. Joint Director Information Syed Shahnawaz Bukhari said the administration is working to revive J&K's cinematic legacy, with more than 360 delegates from outside J&K attending screenings, expert sessions and industry programs.

The programming doubles as economic policy. A sustained return of film productions would mean work for local transport, hotels, catering, technicians, location managers and performers — which is why the festival pairs spectacle with masterclasses intended to build a local creative ecosystem rather than just entertain a crowd for four days.

Diaspora Angle

For diaspora audiences who grew up on these same classics, the floating cinema lands on a nerve: the films that once sold Kashmir to the world are now being shown on the water where many of them were filmed. Kashmir watching films about the Kashmir it once was, in the middle of the landscape that made those films famous — it is a reminder of a shared cinematic inheritance that travels well beyond the Valley.

What's Next

The open question is whether the floating screen outlives the festival. Organizers have not announced a permanent program, and any expansion would have to reckon with Dal Lake's environmental sensitivity — conservation, waste management and crowd control all constrain what the lake can absorb. For now, the closing screening of Kabhi Kabhie on September 10 will determine whether this edition of the floating cinema ends as a one-off spectacle or becomes the start of a summer tradition.
